Temporal Graph Benchmarks In recent years, significant progress has been made toward standardising evaluation in temporal graph link prediction, most notably through the Temporal Graph Benchmark (TGB) [ 82 ] and its extension TGB 2.0 [ 83 ] on multi-relational and heterogeneous temporal graphs. These benchmarks provide datasets, unified preprocessing pipelines, and public leaderboards, 1 enabling systematic comparisons among a wide range of methods. TGB includes datasets from diverse domains. For example, a dataset on Wikipedia co-editing interactions focuses on predicting which page a user will edit at a given time [ 84 ]. Another dataset on Amazon product reviews considers the task of predicting the next product a user will review [ 85 ]. A financial dataset based on stablecoin ERC20 transactions requires forecasting the destination address of a transfer, including cases during the Terra Luna collapse [ 86 ]. A social media dataset constructed from Reddit reply dynamics predicts whether one user will respond to another [ 87 ]. Finally, a dataset on international flights predicts whether a flight will occur between two airports on a specified day [ 88 ]. Collectively, these datasets span domains such as collaborative editing, e-commerce, finance, social media, and transportation, highlighting the broad range of real-world applications for TLP. Both TGB and TGB 2.0 report systematic comparisons of TLP methods, ranging from classical heuristics and static baselines to state-of-the-art temporal graph neural networks such as JODIE, TGN, and CAW. The leaderboard results highlight that while sophisticated temporal models often achieve strong predictive performance, simple memory-based heuristics also remain competitive, especially on large-scale datasets. Summary Building on the distinctions introduced in the previous section, this taxonomy frames TLP methods around two complementary units: the Representation Unit and the Inference Unit. The Representation Unit reflects the discrete-time vs continuous-time modelling paradigm, focusing on how temporal networks are represented and encoded. The Inference Unit corresponds to the transductive vs inductive inference setting, determining how predictions are carried out given the learned representations. By combining these two dimensions, we categorise existing methods into four principal groups, providing a coherent structure for understanding these approaches. This design not only ensures consistency with the conceptual foundations of temporal networks but also highlights open challenges, such as bridging hybrid Representation and Inference Units, balancing representational fidelity and efficiency, and enabling models to generalise across diverse TLP scenarios. Review of Representation Units for TLP Discrete-time Dynamic Graphs Methods Snapshots The Snapshots approach is a fundamental method employed in the domain of discrete-time dynamic graphs for TLP. This technique directly inputs network temporal adjacency matrices into the inference unit. The snapshots are treated as a sequence of static networks and are structurally represented by adjacency matrices. This method is effective for tasks that resemble time-series inference. The direct use of snapshots simplifies the representation and processing of dynamic graphs, making it an efficient choice for many application scenarios. Feature Extraction Node-based Similarity Approaches Entities tend to form new connections with highly similar to themselves. Node neighbourhoods are crucial in similarity calculation. Building on this observation, researchers have developed neighbour-based methods that utilise neighbourhood topological information from discrete snapshots for TLP.
